title: Human Impact on the Environment
seo_title: SSS 3 Biology: Human Impact on the Environment Worksheets (WAEC/NECO)
standard_code: SSS 3 Biology: Human Impact on the Environment
standard_text: Human influences on the atmosphere (the greenhouse effect, climate change, ozone depletion); water availability and quality; food security; loss of biodiversity (habitat destruction, poaching, alien invasive species); solid waste; sustainable practices. (summary of the senior secondary Biology curriculum, SSS 3; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 3 Biology worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): the greenhouse effect, human activities and ecosystems, pollution and toxins, loss of biodiversity and sustainable practices. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Burning fossil fuels adds CO₂, which enhances the greenhouse effect.
key_sub: Alien invasive plants use a lot of water and replace indigenous plants.
body_html:
How to think about it

Burning coal and petrol releases carbon dioxide, which traps more heat and causes global warming and climate change. CFCs damage the ozone layer, which protects us from UV radiation. Water is polluted by sewage, fertilisers, industry and acid mine drainage.

Biodiversity is lost through habitat destruction, hunting for bushmeat, over-exploitation and alien invasive species such as water hyacinth in rivers and lagoons. Food security needs sustainable farming. Reducing, reusing and recycling waste, and conserving water and energy help protect the environment.

Example

Why are alien plants such as water hyacinth removed?

Water and indigenous plants

Answer: they use lots of water and outcompete indigenous plants

Example

Which gas mainly causes the enhanced greenhouse effect?

From burning fuels

Answer: carbon dioxide

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the greenhouse effect itself is bad (without it Earth would be too cold).
  • Mixing up the ozone hole and global warming.
  • Thinking recycling is the only way to reduce waste.

faq.q: What is the Great Green Wall?
faq.a: A plan to plant trees and restore land across the Sahel, including northern Nigeria, to stop the desert from spreading.

faq.q: How does climate change affect food security?
faq.a: Droughts, floods and higher temperatures reduce crop yields.

items.q: Large areas of ice melt, exposing dark ocean. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.q: Using Ada's graph, how much did CO₂ increase from 1960 to 2010?
Femi asks what is mainly causing the rise shown in the graph. What is the best answer?
c: people burning fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas
more sunlight from a closer sun
items.e: Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ that was stored underground for millions of years.

items.q: Using Yusuf's graph, how much did CO₂ increase from 1960 to 2020?
Which greenhouse gas is mainly increased by burning wood?
items.e: Methane: cattle, rice, landfill. Carbon dioxide: burning fuels, deforestation.

items.q: Using Victor's graph, how much did CO₂ increase from 1980 to 2020?
Which greenhouse gas is mainly increased by burning fossil fuels?
items.e: Methane: cattle, rice, landfill. Carbon dioxide: burning fuels, deforestation.

items.q: Usman's class is studying causes of global warming. How does landfills full of rotting rubbish contribute?
c: It does not affect the air.
It adds methane, a greenhouse gas, to the air.
It makes a hole in the ozone layer that lets in heat.
It makes Earth closer to the sun.
items.e: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

items.q: Nkechi's class is studying causes of global warming. How does heating homes with natural gas contribute?
c: It adds carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas, to the air.
It makes Earth closer to the sun.
It makes a hole in the ozone layer that lets in heat.
It does not affect the air.
items.e: Greenhouse gases trap heat in the atmosphere.

items.q: Which greenhouse gas is mainly increased by rice paddy fields?
items.e: Methane: cattle, rice, landfill. Carbon dioxide: burning fuels, deforestation.

items.q: More CO₂ and methane in the atmosphere. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.e: Methane: cattle, rice, landfill. Carbon dioxide: burning fuels, deforestation.

c: driving electric cars charged with clean energy

c: using solar and wind energy instead of coal
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: Deforestation releases stored carbon. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.q: Blessing graphed carbon dioxide (CO₂) measured at Mauna Loa, Hawaii. What trend does it show?
c: CO₂ in the air has been increasing.
CO₂ in the air has been decreasing.
CO₂ went up and down randomly.
items.e: Each later year has a higher value.

items.q: Obinna's class wants to reduce greenhouse gases. Which action would help?
c: cycling or walking for short trips
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: Chidi's class wants to reduce greenhouse gases. Which action would help?
items.e: This reduces greenhouse gases or removes CO₂ from the air.

items.q: A large eruption puts sulfur particles in the stratosphere. Does this tend to warm or cool the climate?
c: it only changes weather for one day
items.e: More energy kept in → warming; less energy in or more reflected → cooling.

items.q: Bayo reads: “A volcano covers land with ash.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Uche reads: “A flood covers a river valley with mud.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Zainab's class studies this problem: “Cars and factories burn fossil fuels.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertiliser
public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
cooling the water in ponds before it is released
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Abdullahi observes: “A factory releases hot water into a lake.” What impact can this have?
c: warmer water with less oxygen for fish
algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Peter's class studies this problem: “A factory releases hot water into a lake.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertiliser
cooling the water in ponds before it is released
reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Uju observes: “Forests are cleared for new houses.” What impact can this have?
c: algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
warmer water with less oxygen for fish
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Samuel learns: Sea otters were overhunted. What happened to the sea urchins?
c: They increased and ate the kelp forests.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: Bisi's class studies this problem: “Fertiliser runs off farms into a river.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: cooling the water in ponds before it is released
reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
rain gardens and permeable pavement that soak up runoff
planting grass buffer strips along the river and using less fertiliser
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Abdullahi wants to know whether a recycling programme reduces rubbish. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: ask one neighbour what they think
weigh the rubbish sent to the landfill each week before and after
check once on a single day
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Ikenna observes: “Rainwater carries oil and rubbish from car parks into streams.” What impact can this have?
c: animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
warmer water with less oxygen for fish
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Kelechi reads: “Kudzu vines spread over forests in the South.” Is this a change to a physical (nonliving) or biological (living) part of the ecosystem?
items.e: Physical parts include water, soil, temperature and fire; biological parts are living things.

items.q: Tobi wants to know whether a new bus line reduces air pollution. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: ask one neighbour what they think
check once on a single day
measure air quality and traffic for several months before and after
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Esther wants to know whether a rain garden reduces stream pollution. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: ask one neighbour what they think
check once on a single day
measure pollution in the stream before and after the rain garden is built
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Victor wants to know whether a wildlife bridge reduces animal deaths. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: count animals hit on the road before and after the bridge
ask one neighbour what they think
check once on a single day
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Gbenga observes: “Cars and factories burn fossil fuels.” What impact can this have?
c: warmer water with less oxygen for fish
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Chidi wants to know whether fewer fish die after a farm uses less fertiliser. What is the best way to monitor this?
c: check once on a single day
ask one neighbour what they think
count fish and measure oxygen in the river over several years
items.e: Monitoring uses measurements over time, before and after.

items.q: Nonso learns: A disease killed many bats. What happened to the night-flying insects?
c: They increased because fewer bats ate them.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: Esther learns: A drought dried a pond. What happened to the frogs?
c: They decreased because they lost water and food.
They moved into the trees permanently.
items.e: A change to one part of an ecosystem affects other populations.

items.q: Chidi's class studies this problem: “Plastic bags blow into the ocean.” Which solution would best reduce the impact?
c: reusable bags and bans on single-use plastic
rain gardens and permeable pavement that soak up runoff
public transit, electric vehicles and cleaner power
keeping protected green spaces and wildlife corridors
items.e: A good solution targets the cause of the impact.

items.q: Babatunde observes: “Plastic bags blow into the ocean.” What impact can this have?
c: animals swallowing or getting tangled in plastic
warmer water with less oxygen for fish
air pollution and more carbon dioxide
algae blooms that use up oxygen and kill fish
items.e: Human activities can change Earth's systems.

items.q: Which is a benefit of buying local food?
c: less fuel is used to transport it
items.e: Shorter trips mean fewer emissions.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by chemicals from a factory poured into a river?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the water.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by rubbish thrown into a canal?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the water.

items.q: What does the Indigenous idea of 'Seven Generations' teach?
c: to think about how our decisions will affect people seven generations from now
items.e: It is a long-term view of sustainability.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by litter left on a beach?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the land.

items.q: How can fertiliser runoff harm a lake?
c: It causes algae to grow quickly, and when the algae die, oxygen levels drop.
items.e: This is called eutrophication.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by burning forests that cause haze?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the air.

items.q: What could happen to apple harvests if bee numbers fall a lot?
c: Fewer flowers are pollinated, so fewer apples grow.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: Why are wetlands called 'the kidneys of the landscape'?
items.e: Wetlands also reduce flooding.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by plastic bags left in a park?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the land.

items.q: What is sustainability?
c: using resources as fast as possible
meeting our needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs
items.e: Sustainable choices protect ecosystems.

items.q: Which is an example of habitat restoration?
c: removing all trees from a park
replanting native plants along a stream bank
items.e: Restored habitats support wildlife.

items.q: What is an ecological footprint?
c: the amount of land and resources needed to support a person's lifestyle
items.e: Smaller footprints are more sustainable.

items.q: What is interdependence?
c: Living things in an ecosystem depend on each other for food, shelter and pollination.
items.e: Plants and animals depend on each other.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by aircraft taking off near homes?
items.e: Loud sounds disturb people and animals.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by detergent washed into a drain?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the water.

items.q: How does urban sprawl affect ecosystems?
c: It replaces natural habitats with roads and buildings.
items.e: Green spaces help reduce the impact.

items.q: Which kind of pollution is caused by smoke from a ship's engine at sea?
items.e: The pollutant goes into the air.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: sulfur dioxide from coal plants causing acid rain?
c: cover crops and buffer strips of plants
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.

items.q: Which action improves soil health on a farm?
c: packing the soil with heavy machines
adding compost and keeping plants growing on the soil
items.e: Organic matter feeds soil organisms and helps the soil hold water.

items.q: Why does using less fertiliser protect lakes?
c: extra nitrogen and phosphorus wash into water and cause algal blooms
fertiliser adds too much salt to the ocean
items.e: When the algae die, decomposers use up the oxygen, and fish can die.

items.q: Nkechi's class studies this problem: “Bee populations are falling near farms.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
c: plant wildflower strips and reduce pesticide use
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: What is a carbon sink?
c: something that takes in more carbon dioxide than it releases, such as a forest or the ocean
items.e: Oceans, soils and forests remove CO₂ from the atmosphere.

items.q: Which human impact are drip irrigation designed to reduce?
c: sulfur dioxide from coal plants causing acid rain
highways cutting animals off from their habitat
farms wasting water through flood irrigation
items.e: Match the solution to the problem.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: landfill chemicals leaking into groundwater?
c: wildlife crossings over or under roads
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.

items.q: What is the Three Sisters planting method?
c: planting three rows of the same crop
watering crops three times a day
growing corn, beans and squash together so each plant helps the others
items.e: Corn supports the beans, beans add nitrogen and squash leaves shade the soil and keep moisture in.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: oil spills from tankers?
c: wildlife crossings over or under roads
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.

items.q: Which human impact are scrubbers in smokestacks designed to reduce?
c: car exhaust releasing carbon monoxide and smog gases
sulfur dioxide from coal plants causing acid rain
dams blocking salmon from swimming upstream
items.e: Match the solution to the problem.

items.q: Why does cutting down a forest add to climate change?
c: fewer trees take in CO₂, and burning or rotting wood releases stored carbon
forests block greenhouse gases from reaching space
trees produce carbon dioxide in photosynthesis
items.e: Forests are carbon sinks; removing them turns a sink into a source.

items.q: Funke's class studies this problem: “Forest animals are trapped in small patches between farms.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
c: connect the patches with wildlife corridors
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: Which is an example of adapting to climate change rather than slowing it?
c: switching from coal to wind power
building higher flood walls and planting trees for shade in cities
items.e: Mitigation reduces the cause; adaptation reduces the damage.

items.q: Which change reduces greenhouse gas emissions from transportation?
c: taking transit, cycling or using electric vehicles charged from clean electricity
idling the car to keep it warm
items.e: Most transport emissions come from burning petrol and diesel.

items.q: Nonso's class studies this problem: “An invasive vine is smothering native plants.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
c: remove the vine and replant native species
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: What is crop rotation?
c: growing different crops in a field in different years
growing the same crop every year
items.e: Rotation keeps soil healthy, breaks pest cycles and can add nitrogen (with legumes such as beans).

items.q: Hadiza's class studies this problem: “A fish population is shrinking from overfishing.” Which solution would best protect biodiversity?
c: set catch limits and protected zones
items.e: It solves the cause of the problem while protecting species.

items.q: Why does growing beans, peas or clover help the next crop?
c: they make the soil more acidic for good
they remove all water from the soil
they block all sunlight from weeds
bacteria in their roots fix nitrogen, which fertilises the soil
items.e: Legumes reduce the need for synthetic fertiliser.

items.q: How do wetlands help reduce the effects of climate change?
c: they store carbon and soak up floodwater
items.e: Peatlands and marshes hold large amounts of carbon in waterlogged soil.

items.q: Which technology is designed to reduce this impact: dams blocking salmon from swimming upstream?
items.e: Engineers design solutions that reduce harm to natural systems.
